tracks.title: The wiring lives nowhere
tracks.text: Lesson 04 point 2 — tangling. This one is a sub-lesson, under org… and it cashes in a promise the parent made. Here's the opening problem. The wiring lives nowhere. Everyone's agent workflow lives in some YAML or JSON file nobody can read… next to docs nobody trusts… next to code in a repo the doc doesn't even know about. And the wiring — what feeds what, what capabilities each piece needs, when the whole thing runs — that's the most important part of the system… and the part with no home. [curious] The org lesson promised something. Org holds runnable code… tangled out to something real. This page is where that gets weaponized. Because the thing org tangles out to… is not a pile of files. It's a typed plan for a whole system… derived from the document itself.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Tangling is compiling a document into a typed build plan. Source blocks… plus six header args… become a world of components, a list of capability imports, and a dataflow graph — with a schedule and a persistence contract derived along the way. The word is Knuth's. In literate programming, tangle extracts the runnable code from a prose document… and weave renders the human reading. The kernel here keeps both verbs. The twist is what tangle produces. [curious] Classic tangle writes out source files. This one writes out a world — a plan shaped like a typed interface. Components in… capability imports declared… and a graph of who feeds whom. Files… to world. That is the whole move.

tracks.title: Six words on a line
tracks.text: Now — six words on a line. A headline tagged workflow is a world. Its descendants tagged component are its components. And a component is just a name… plus the first source block under it. Everything else about it lives in six header args, written right on the source-block line. Let me read the table aloud, one row at a time, because each arg has a job. First… deps — a comma-split list — which becomes the deps array, consumed by the compiler lanes, crates dot io for Rust and npm for JavaScript. Second… uses — and this is the only repeatable one, each occurrence appends — it becomes the world's imports, and it also feeds the upgrade gate. Third… in — a single value — the input port, consumed by edge matching to find its producer. Fourth… out — a single value — the output port, which becomes an edge, or an export if nobody eats it. Fifth… persist — a bare flag, no value — it marks the component durable, surfaced to the VFS checkpoint contract. And sixth… dir — a single path — the escape hatch, pointing at a real project directory instead of an inline block. [curious] Three deserve a second look. Uses is the only repeatable one — a component touching the network and the VFS writes it twice. Persist takes no value at all… Motoko-style, the runtime keeps the component's memory. And dir points at a real repo with its own Cargo file. Unknown tokens? Silently ignored. The parser is forgiving on purpose.

tracks.title: The signature without the code
tracks.text: Here's the part that earns the whole lesson — the signature without the code. The function that builds a component's signature never reads a single source body. It works only from the header args. And from them, it derives three things. First… imports — the sorted, deduplicated union of every uses across all components. That's the world's capability surface. Second… edges — for every in, find the component whose out matches it exactly… and that pair becomes an edge. The dataflow graph is computed, never drawn. Third… exports — every out that nobody consumed. A terminal output, eaten by no downstream in, leaks up to the world's surface. [excited] And because the signature comes from the prose layer, not the code, the language inside the block is irrelevant to wiring. Let me walk you through the real example as a picture. It's called Nightly digest, and it's three blocks in three languages. Picture a chain of three. First box — Fetch events, written in Rust — it declares it uses the VFS query capability, and it produces a port called events-list. Second box — Summarize, written in JavaScript — it consumes events-list, it uses the LLM complete capability, and it produces summary-string. Third box — Send, written in Go — it consumes summary-string, and it uses the email capability. Now watch the edges appear. Fetch produces events-list… Summarize consumes events-list — so an edge is drawn between them, from two strings meeting. Summarize produces summary-string… Send consumes it — second edge. Send produces nothing, so the chain ends. Up above the chain, every uses pooled into three imports — email, LLM complete, and VFS query. And exports… is empty. Because both outputs were consumed inside the world. [curious] Nobody wrote a single edge down. They all fell out of the args.

tracks.title: What comes out
tracks.text: What comes out — it's JSON. Each world carries a name, a schedule, its imports, its exports, its components, its edges, and any nested workflows. The schedule is derived too — a schedule property wins as a cron string, otherwise the org SCHEDULED timestamp becomes a start time, a repeat, and an active flag. And you can run this locally, with no server at all. Let me read you the real output of running tangle on the nightly digest file. The name is Nightly digest. The schedule says it starts on June sixth at six in the morning, repeats every one day, and is active. The imports list three capabilities — LLM complete, email, and VFS query. The exports list… is empty. Then the components, the first of which is Fetch events — language Rust, uses VFS query, no input, output events-list, not persistent, no deps. And finally the edges — two of them — from Fetch events to Summarize, and from Summarize to Send. [excited] Now here's the load-bearing fact. Those edges were written nowhere in the document. They are out events-list meeting in events-list… and summary-string meeting its twin. The exports array is empty because every output found a consumer. Add an out called digest-string to Send… and the world grows an export. That output now leaks to the surface. And removing it later would trip the upgrade gate — because exports may grow… but never shrink. The same surface that wires the system… governs how it evolves.

tracks.title: The plan, executed
tracks.text: Now a depth rung — the plan, executed. This one's skippable, but it's where the plan stops being a document and becomes infrastructure. The runtime schedules the components in topological waves. Each wave is the set of components whose producers are all satisfied… and within a wave, the steps run in parallel — up to eight at once. The edges are plumbing — a producer's standard output pipes into its consumer's standard input. Let me walk the sequence as a story of three waves falling out of two edges. Wave one is Fetch events — it has no producer, so it runs first, on the workflow's own input, and it emits events-list on its standard output. That output pipes straight into Summarize's standard input… which unblocks wave two. Summarize emits summary-string, which pipes into Send… unblocking wave three. And Send is terminal — it produces no output, so the chain ends there. [curious] Each component builds through a content-addressed cache, keyed over its language, its source, and its deps — so a block that hasn't changed is never rebuilt. Two special steps to name. A component whose language is agent runs the agent loop instead of a compiled binary — its source block becomes the system prompt, and the piped input is the task. And the composition is honestly untyped today — it's standard-in to standard-out filters, not typed linking. The typed version, called wac plug, is the named upgrade. One more thing — cycles don't deadlock. An unresolvable remainder gets dumped into one final wave… rather than hanging.

tracks.title: Two args that punch up
tracks.text: Two args that punch above their weight. Both depth rungs. First… dir — the literate document citing a real repository. Instead of an inline block, the component names a project directory… and the sandbox builds that project on its own terms. For Rust, the kernel parses the project's Cargo file dependencies — skipping optional, git, and path deps — then runs the in-sandbox toolchain. Native cargo is never invoked. Let me read the org for it. A component headline called Scrape pages, tagged component… then a Rust source block whose header says dir, tools-slash-scraper, and out, pages-json. So the doc cites a real repo… that repo's Cargo file owns the deps… the sandbox builds it… and native cargo never runs. The component is a whole project, referenced from one line of prose. Second… persist — the persistence contract. It's a bare flag. And a function called durable-components walks the plan — worlds and nested sub-workflows — and returns the names of every component carrying it. Read the org. A headline called Remember, tagged component, with a Rust block whose header says persist and out memory-json. For that plan, durable-components returns a list of one — Remember — the runtime's list of who survives a redeploy. [curious] But be precise. Components are stateless between runs by default. The persistence substrate is the VFS… not raw linear memory. Persist is the contract that the component checkpoints its state to the VFS… which freeze and resume copy, and which replication keeps durable. The VFS is the orthogonal-persistence layer. No magic memory snapshots.

tracks.title: The plan you can refuse
tracks.text: The plan you can refuse. Before anything builds, the plan can be validated — and validation runs with no server, the same native kernel as tangle. It makes exactly two checks per workflow. First check — a component with no source block, no language at all — that's an error, the component is missing a body. Second check — an input with no upstream producer — also an error, with the message, input X has no upstream producer. Let me show you the second one, live. The broken workflow is a single component that consumes events-list… with nothing producing it. Run lint on it, and you get back one diagnostic — level error, scope Summarize, message, input events-list has no upstream producer. [excited] That is a test suite running against a document. The org lesson made a claim — you can't write a test suite for Markdown. This is that claim, cashed in. A dangling input is a checkable fact… named and scoped… before a single line of code compiles. And the same derived signature does deploy-time duty too. A second gate compares two versions of a world — a removed export is an error, exports may grow but never shrink… a new import is a warning, a new capability is now required… a changed output type is an error. That gate belongs to the nesting lesson. The point here is only that it reads the same signature surface this page taught. One signature… two jobs. Wiring the system… and governing how it changes.

tracks.title: Where the seams are
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the seams are. The model is real, but young, and the edges are sharp in named places. First… edges match by exact string. The type half of a port name is an opaque label the kernel never parses. There's no real type system on the wire yet — wac plug is the named upgrade. Second… duplicate producers. If two components declare the same out, the last one silently wins. Validate does not catch it. Third… deps is honored for Rust and JavaScript only. Other languages ignore deps for now — stated outright in the source. Fourth… uses is signature-truth, but not yet a grant. Today it feeds the imports and the upgrade warning. It does not yet wire per-component capability grants — search the runtime for it and you get nothing. An honest seam, marked as one. And fifth… cycles get lumped, not rejected — an unresolvable remainder is dumped into one final wave so nothing deadlocks. [curious] None of these are hidden. They're the gap between the typed-world compiler that exists today… and the one the architecture is pointed at. And that gap is exactly the roadmap.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this just org-babel? No — there's no execute-in-editor step. The kernel compiles the document into a plan… the engine runs the plan later, in a sandbox. Tangling is the compile half. Do I write this JSON by hand? Never. The plan is derived, not configured. You write org with source blocks and header args… and tangle is a read-only derivation that emits the JSON. Is events-list a real type? Not yet — it's an opaque contract string, matched by exact string. Can a component be a whole repository? Yes — that's dir, pointing at a real project the sandbox builds on its own terms. And where do the tangled files go? [chuckles] Nowhere. That's the twist. Knuth's tangle wrote files out to disk. This tangle writes out a world — a plan describing components, imports, and a graph. There are no extracted files to manage… because the document already is the source.

tracks.title: Back up to org
tracks.text: So that's tangling. Six words on a source block… and the document becomes a typed world. Components, a capability import list, a dataflow graph, a schedule — all derived from the prose layer… never the code. Which is exactly why one workflow can mix Rust, JavaScript, and Go and still compile to one thing. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is a sub-lesson under org — lesson four — the grammar that makes the whole derivation possible. Go back there for why the document is parseable at all. And from there, workflows — lesson eight — is the plan side this page is the compiler under. The interface lives in the prose. The language doesn't matter. That's the whole lesson.
